claim: Lactoferrin-binding protein B (LbpB) is a lipoprotein present on the surface of Neisseria.
source: Lactoferrin-binding protein B (LbpB) is a lipoprotein present on the surface of Neisseria that has been postulated to serve dual functions during pathogenesis in both iron acquisition from lactoferrin (Lf), and in providing protection against the cationic antimicrobial peptide lactoferricin (Lfcn).
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as an established fact about LbpB.

claim: LbpB has been postulated to serve dual functions during pathogenesis in both iron acquisition from lactoferrin and in providing protection against the cationic antimicrobial peptide lactoferricin.
source: Lactoferrin-binding protein B (LbpB) is a lipoprotein present on the surface of Neisseria that has been postulated to serve dual functions during pathogenesis in both iron acquisition from lactoferrin (Lf), and in providing protection against the cationic antimicrobial peptide lactoferricin (Lfcn).
evidence: This claim is supported by references to previous studies and the current work's findings.

claim: LbpB from N. meningitidis and N. gonorrhoeae forms a 1:1 complex with human holo-Lf.
source: Here, we present the structures of LbpB from N. meningitidis and N. gonorrhoeae in complex with human holo-Lf, forming a 1:1 complex and confirmed by size-exclusion chromatography small-angle X-ray scattering.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from SEC, SAXS, crystal structure, and cryoEM structure as described in the manuscript.

claim: LbpB consists of N- and C-lobes with the N-lobe interacting extensively with the C-lobe of Lf.
source: LbpB consists of N- and C-lobes with the N-lobe interacting extensively with the C-lobe of Lf.
evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal and cryoEM structures presented in the manuscript.

claim: Lf and Lfcn bind independently to LbpB.
source: Our structures provide insight into LbpB's preference towards holo-Lf, and our mutagenesis and binding studies show that Lf and Lfcn bind independently.
evidence: This is supported by mutagenesis studies and ITC binding experiments showing non-overlapping binding sites.

claim: LbpB serves to capture and preserve Lf in an iron-bound state for delivery to the membrane transporter LbpA for iron piracy.
source: Our studies provide the molecular details for how LbpB serves to capture and preserve Lf in an iron-bound state for delivery to the membrane transporter LbpA for iron piracy, and as an antimicrobial peptide sink to evade host immune defenses.
evidence: This is supported by structural data showing LbpB's interaction with holo-Lf and comparison with the Tbp system.

claim: LbpB serves as an antimicrobial peptide sink to evade host immune defenses.
source: Our studies provide the molecular details for how LbpB serves to capture and preserve Lf in an iron-bound state for delivery to the membrane transporter LbpA for iron piracy, and as an antimicrobial peptide sink to evade host immune defenses.
evidence: This is supported by binding studies with Lfcn and previous literature on LbpB's role in neutralizing antimicrobial peptides.

claim: There are 17 species of Neisseria that colonize humans with only two being pathogenic, N. meningitidis and N. gonorrhoeae.
source: There are 17 species of Neisseria that colonize humans with only two being pathogenic, N. meningitidis and N. gonorrhoeae (Seifert, 2019; Tone Tønjum, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: N. meningitidis asymptomatically colonizes ~10% of the world's population.
source: N. meningitidis asymptomatically colonizes ~10% of the world's population, however, once pathogenic can lead to meningitidis and sepsis and lead to high fatality rates in the absence of immediate treatment (Caugant and Brynildsrud, 2020; Read, 2019; Siddiqui et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to epidemiological studies.

claim: N. meningitidis can lead to meningitidis and sepsis with high fatality rates in the absence of immediate treatment.
source: N. meningitidis asymptomatically colonizes ~10% of the world's population, however, once pathogenic can lead to meningitidis and sepsis and lead to high fatality rates in the absence of immediate treatment (Caugant and Brynildsrud, 2020; Read, 2019; Siddiqui et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to clinical literature.

claim: N. gonorrhoeae causes the sexually transmitted disease gonorrhoea.
source: N. gonorrhoeae causes the sexually transmitted disease gonorrhoea (Boyajian et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The CDC has categorized N. gonorrhoeae as an urgent threat to public health.
source: The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) have categorized N. gonorrhoeae as an urgent threat to public health, which requires immediate and aggressive actions to combat the emerging antibiotic-resistant strains recently discovered (Aitolo et al., 2021; Prevention (CDC), 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to CDC reports.

claim: Vaccines are now available against all pathogenic serogroups of N. meningitidis.
source: Although vaccines are now available against all pathogenic serogroups of N. meningitidis, there are well-documented drawbacks and limitations of these vaccines (Deasy and Read, 2011; Pizza et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to vaccine literature.

claim: There are well-documented drawbacks and limitations of vaccines against N. meningitidis.
source: Although vaccines are now available against all pathogenic serogroups of N. meningitidis, there are well-documented drawbacks and limitations of these vaccines (Deasy and Read, 2011; Pizza et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to vaccine literature.

claim: There is no vaccine against gonococcal infections despite decades of research.
source: And despite decades of research, there is still no vaccine against gonococcal infections.
evidence: This is stated as an established fact in the field.

claim: Iron is an essential nutrient for survival, growth, and virulence of Neisseria.
source: Iron is an essential nutrient for survival, growth, and virulence (Grifantini et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Free iron is essentially non-existent in the human host.
source: Given that free iron is essentially non-existent in the human host, Neisseria have evolved specialized surface receptors to hijack iron from host iron-binding proteins such as transferrin (Tf) and lactoferrin (Lf) (Lee and Schryvers, 1988; Schryvers and Lee, 1989; Schryvers and Morris, 1988; Yadav et al., 2019).
evidence: This is established knowledge about iron availability in the human host.

claim: Neisseria have evolved specialized surface receptors to hijack iron from host iron-binding proteins such as transferrin and lactoferrin.
source: Given that free iron is essentially non-existent in the human host, Neisseria have evolved specialized surface receptors to hijack iron from host iron-binding proteins such as transferrin (Tf) and lactoferrin (Lf) (Lee and Schryvers, 1988; Schryvers and Lee, 1989; Schryvers and Morris, 1988; Yadav et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: The transferrin-binding protein (Tbp) system consists of a TonB-dependent transporter called TbpA and a lipoprotein co-receptor called TbpB.
source: One of the more well-studied metal acquisition systems in Neisseria is the transferrin-binding protein (Tbp) system, which consists of an a TonB-dependent transporter called TbpA and a lipoprotein co-receptor called TbpB (Cornelissen et al., 1992; Irwin et al., 1993; Noinaj et al., 2012a; Noinaj et al., 2012b; Noinaj et al., 2010; Pintor et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: TbpB serves to capture and deliver iron-loaded Tf to TbpA for iron extraction and import across the outer membrane.
source: Here, TbpB serves to capture and deliver iron-loaded Tf to TbpA for iron extraction and import across the outer membrane in a process that requires energy from the Ton complex at the inner membrane (Cornelissen et al., 1992; Cornelissen and Hollander, 2011; Noinaj et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The lactoferrin-binding protein (Lbp) system is composed of LbpA and LbpB and targets Lf as an iron source.
source: A second analogous system is called the lactoferrin-binding protein (Lbp) system, which is composed of LbpA and LbpB, targets Lf as an iron source (Figure 1A; Biswas and Sparling, 1995; Gray-Owen and Schryvers, 1996; Lee and Schryvers, 1988; Noinaj et al., 2013; Schryvers et al., 1998; Schryvers and Morris, 1988).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature and Figure 1A.

claim: No structures of Lbp proteins in complex with Lf have been reported prior to this study.
source: However, less is known structurally and functionally about the Lbp system as no structures of Lbp proteins in complex with Lf have been reported.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in the literature that this study addresses.

claim: All strains of N. meningitidis contain a functional Lbp system.
source: While all strains of N. meningitidis contain a functional Lbp system, it is only observed in roughly half of the N. gonorrhoeae strains (Anderson et al., 2003; Biswas et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The Lbp system is only observed in roughly half of the N. gonorrhoeae strains.
source: While all strains of N. meningitidis contain a functional Lbp system, it is only observed in roughly half of the N. gonorrhoeae strains (Anderson et al., 2003; Biswas et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The Lbp system may serve as a backup option to the Tbp system to assist in mediating pathogenesis within diverse host environments.
source: Studies hint that the Lbp system may serve as a backup option to the Tbp system to assist in mediating pathogenesis within diverse host environments, as a Neisserial strain lacking the Tbp proteins were still able to use the Lbp proteins to cause infection (Anderson et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study showing functional redundancy.

claim: A Neisserial strain lacking the Tbp proteins was still able to use the Lbp proteins to cause infection.
source: Studies hint that the Lbp system may serve as a backup option to the Tbp system to assist in mediating pathogenesis within diverse host environments, as a Neisserial strain lacking the Tbp proteins were still able to use the Lbp proteins to cause infection (Anderson et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous experimental study.

claim: A strain expressing both Tbp and Lbp systems was more competitive than a strain expressing just the Tbp system alone.
source: Further, it was also shown that a strain expressing both systems was more competitive than a strain expressing just the Tbp system alone (Anderson et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous experimental study.

claim: Anti-sera raised against the Lbp proteins displays bactericidal activity.
source: Moreover, anti-sera raised against the Lbp proteins displays bactericidal activity, exemplifying the promise of this system as a target for therapeutic intervention (Pettersson et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous experimental study.

claim: LbpB is predicted to have a similar domain organization to TbpB consisting of N- and C-lobes, with each lobe composed of an eight-stranded β-barrel sitting adjacent to a handle domain.
source: Given its sequence homology to TbpB, LbpB is predicted to have a similar domain organization consisting of an N- and C-lobes, with each lobe composed of an eight-stranded β-barrel sitting adjacent to a handle domain (Beddek and Schryvers, 2010; Brooks et al., 2014; Ekins et al., 2004; Lee and Schryvers, 1988; Noinaj et al., 2013; Ostan et al., 2017; Schryvers and Lee, 1989).
evidence: This is based on sequence homology and supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The structure of the N-lobe of LbpB has been reported, showing conservation with the N-lobe of TbpB.
source: This was partially confirmed when the structure of the N-lobe of LbpB was reported, showing conservation with the N-lobe of TbpB (Brooks et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous structural study.

claim: Docking studies predicted that N-lobe of Lf interacts with LbpB.
source: Docking studies predicted that N-lobe of Lf interacts with LbpB (Arutyunova et al., 2012; Brooks et al., 2014), while hydrogen-deuterium exchange studies, combined with site-directed mutagenesis, showed that the C-lobe of Lf interacts with LbpB (Ostan et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous computational studies.

claim: Hydrogen-deuterium exchange studies, combined with site-directed mutagenesis, showed that the C-lobe of Lf interacts with LbpB.
source: Docking studies predicted that N-lobe of Lf interacts with LbpB (Arutyunova et al., 2012; Brooks et al., 2014), while hydrogen-deuterium exchange studies, combined with site-directed mutagenesis, showed that the C-lobe of Lf interacts with LbpB (Ostan et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous experimental study.

claim: LbpB has been shown to provide protection against the host cationic antimicrobial peptide lactoferricin (Lfcn), an 11-residue metabolized fragment from the N-lobe of Lf.
source: In addition to its role in iron acquisition, LbpB has been shown to provide protection against the host cationic antimicrobial peptide lactoferricin (Lfcn), an 11-residue metabolized fragment from the N-lobe of Lf (Figure 1A; Morgenthau et al., 2014a; Morgenthau et al., 2012; Morgenthau et al., 2014b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature and Figure 1A.

claim: One model proposes that Lfcn binds along the N-lobe of LbpB.
source: Studies have been conflicting on exactly where LbpB interacts with Lfcn to neutralize this threat. One model proposes that it binds along the N-lobe (Brooks et al., 2014), while another model points to several anionic regions along the C-lobe (Morgenthau et al., 2014a; Morgenthau et al., 2014b).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Another model points to several anionic regions along the C-lobe of LbpB as the Lfcn binding site.
source: Studies have been conflicting on exactly where LbpB interacts with Lfcn to neutralize this threat. One model proposes that it binds along the N-lobe (Brooks et al., 2014), while another model points to several anionic regions along the C-lobe (Morgenthau et al., 2014a; Morgenthau et al., 2014b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: LbpB can be proteolytically cleaved by NalP, which enables it to diffuse into the host environment to pre-emptively neutralize Lfcn.
source: In addition to protecting the surface of Neisseria directly, LbpB has been shown to also be proteolytically cleaved by NalP, which enables it to diffuse into the host environment to pre-emptively neutralize Lfcn (Roussel-Jazédé et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Purified LbpB constructs (NmLbpB residues 20-737 and NgLbpB residues 20-728) were sufficient for binding holo-Lf.
source: Solid-phase-binding assays showed that these purified LbpB constructs were sufficient for binding holo-Lf (Figure 1C and Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: SDS-PAGE analysis confirmed that NmLbpB and NgLbpB form 1:1 stoichiometric complexes with Lf.
source: Sodium dodecyl sulphate-polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis (SDS–PAGE) analysis confirmed the peak contained both components and suggested a 1:1 stoichiometric complex for both the NmLbpB and NgLbpB complexes with Lf (Figure 1E and Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: NmLbpB appears to form a stable 1:1 complex with Lf as observed by SEC.
source: However, in our studies with complex formation by SEC, we observed that NmLbpB appears to form a stable 1:1 complex with Lf.
evidence: This is supported by experimental SEC data.

claim: SEC-SAXS studies showed that individual LbpB and Lf proteins existed as monomers in solution.
source: For our experiments here, our SEC-SAXS studies showed that the individual LbpB and Lf proteins existed as monomers in solution, while the NmLbpB–Lf complex had an experimental molecular weight of 159.6 kDa corresponding to 1:1 stoichiometry complex of NmLbpB and Lf (calculated molecular weight is 156.6 kDa) (Figure 2A and B and Supplementary file 1a).
evidence: This is supported by SEC-SAXS experimental data shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: The NmLbpB–Lf complex had an experimental molecular weight of 159.6 kDa corresponding to 1:1 stoichiometry (calculated molecular weight is 156.6 kDa).
source: For our experiments here, our SEC-SAXS studies showed that the individual LbpB and Lf proteins existed as monomers in solution, while the NmLbpB–Lf complex had an experimental molecular weight of 159.6 kDa corresponding to 1:1 stoichiometry complex of NmLbpB and Lf (calculated molecular weight is 156.6 kDa) (Figure 2A and B and Supplementary file 1a).
evidence: This is supported by SEC-SAXS experimental data.

claim: NgLbpB alone and in complex with Lf match closely to NmLbpB in solution as shown by SEC-SAXS analysis.
source: Further, we used SEC-SAXS analysis to show that in solution, NgLbpB alone and a complex with Lf match closely to those with NmLbpB (Figure 2A and B, and SI Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by SEC-SAXS experimental data shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: The crystal structure of NmLbpB in complex with Lf was solved to 2.85 Å resolution.
source: Data were collected at the GM/CA ID-D beamline at the Advanced Photon Source and the structure of the NmLbpB–Lf complex solved to 2.85 Å resolution using molecular replacement in space group P43212.
evidence: This is supported by crystallographic data collection and structure determination.

claim: The NmLbpB–Lf crystal structure was refined to final Rwork/Rfree values of 0.20/0.25.
source: Model building was performed in COOT and the structure refined using phenix.refine to final Rwork/Rfree values of 0.20/0.25 (Figure 3A and Supplementary file 1b).
evidence: This is supported by crystallographic refinement statistics.

claim: The NmLbpB–Lf complex structure contains one molecule of Lf (consisting of ordered N- and C-lobes) and one molecule of NmLbpB (consisting of an ordered N-lobe, but partially ordered C-lobe).
source: One complex was observed in the structure containing one molecule of Lf (consisting of ordered N- and C-lobes) and one molecule of NmLbpB (consisting of an ordered N-lobe, but partially ordered C-lobe).
evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure.

claim: The overall structure of the NmLbpB–Lf complex has an overall L-shape.
source: The overall structure of the NmLbpB–Lf complex has an overall L-shape (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The N-lobe of NmLbpB is composed of residues 1–342 forming two domains, an N-terminal handle domain (residues 45–173) and an eight-stranded β-barrel domain (residues 174–342).
source: The N-lobe of NmLbpB is composed of residues 1–342 forming two domains, an N-terminal handle domain (residues 45–173) and an eight-stranded β-barrel domain (residues 174–342).
evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure.

claim: The C-lobe of NmLbpB is composed of residues 359–718 and found largely disordered in the crystal structure.
source: The C-lobe of NmLbpB is composed of residues 359–718 and found largely disordered in the crystal structure as evident from higher B-factors for this region compared to the rest of the structure (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure as shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Structural alignment of Lf alone (PDB ID 2BJJ) with Lf in the NmLbpB–Lf complex shows minimal conformational changes upon binding NmLbpB (RMSD 1.3 Å).
source: Structural alignment of Lf alone (PDB ID 2BJJ) with Lf in our complex (RMSD 1.3 Å) shows that both lobes are in closed conformations, as expected since we observe an iron in each lobe, and that Lf undergoes minimal changes upon binding NmLbpB (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Both lobes of Lf are in closed conformations in the NmLbpB–Lf complex.
source: Structural alignment of Lf alone (PDB ID 2BJJ) with Lf in our complex (RMSD 1.3 Å) shows that both lobes are in closed conformations, as expected since we observe an iron in each lobe, and that Lf undergoes minimal changes upon binding NmLbpB (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure.

claim: The interaction of NmLbpB with Lf is mediated exclusively through the N-lobe of NmLbpB with the C-lobe of Lf.
source: The interaction of NmLbpB with Lf is mediated exclusively through the N-lobe of NmLbpB with the C-lobe of Lf (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The NmLbpB–Lf interface consists of regions along both the C1 and C2 domains of Lf including residues D630, S637, T639, K640 (C1 domain) and E512, R525, E538, N539, D561 (C2 domain).
source: This interface consists of regions along both the C1 and C2 domains of Lf including residues D630, S637, T639, K640 (C1 domain) and E512, R525, E538, N539, D561 (C2 domain) (Figure 3B and E).
evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure shown in Figure 3B and E.

claim: The N-lobe of NmLbpB has an extended interaction interface with Lf that includes residues N154, R193, S201, D204, N213, R223, K230, Y253, Q255, and S258.
source: Interacting simultaneously with the C1 and C2 domains of Lf, the N-lobe of NmLbpB has an extended interaction interface that includes residues N154, R193, S201, D204, N213, R223, K230, Y253, Q255, and S258 (Figure 3B and E).
evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure shown in Figure 3B and E.

claim: Solid-phase-binding assays showed that Lf could only interact with the full length and N-lobe only constructs of NmLbpB, but not with the C-lobe only.
source: Given our crystal structure indicated that binding to Lf was exclusively along the N-lobe of NmLbpB, we used solid-phase-binding assays to show that indeed Lf could only interact with the full length and N-lobe only constructs, but not with the C-lobe only (Figure 3F and Figure 3—source data 1f).
evidence: This is supported by experimental binding assay data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The cryoEM structure of NgLbpB in complex with Lf was determined to 3.65 Å resolution.
source: Crystallization with NgLbpB was unsuccessful, therefore, we used cryoEM to determine the structure of NgLbpB in complex with Lf to 3.65 Å resolution (Supplementary file 1c).
evidence: This is supported by cryoEM data collection and structure determination.

claim: Very good density was observed for side chains of both lobes of Lf and for the N-lobe of NgLbpB in the cryoEM structure.
source: Very good density was observed for side chains of both lobes of Lf and for the N-lobe of NgLbpB allowing unambiguous model building and refinement, however, almost no density was observed for the C-lobe of NgLbpB, unless map contours were reduced drastically (Figure 4A and B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is directly observed in the cryoEM density map shown in Figure 4A and B.

claim: Almost no density was observed for the C-lobe of NgLbpB in the cryoEM structure, unless map contours were reduced drastically.
source: Very good density was observed for side chains of both lobes of Lf and for the N-lobe of NgLbpB allowing unambiguous model building and refinement, however, almost no density was observed for the C-lobe of NgLbpB, unless map contours were reduced drastically (Figure 4A and B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is directly observed in the cryoEM density map.

claim: An alignment of the Nm and NgLbpB complexes with Lf had an overall RMSD of 3.7 Å, but an improved RMSD of 1.4 Å when aligning just along the interacting domains (C-lobe of Lf and N-lobe of LbpB).
source: An alignment of the Nm and NgLbpB complexes with Lf had an overall RMSD of 3.7 Å, however, an improved RMSD of 1.4 Å when aligning just along the interacting domains (C-lobe of Lf and N-lobe of LbpB), indicating a conserved binding interface between Nm and Ng (Figure 4C and D).
evidence: This is supported by structural alignment shown in Figure 4C and D.

claim: The conserved binding interface between Nm and Ng LbpB is indicated by the RMSD of 1.4 Å when aligning the interacting domains.
source: An alignment of the Nm and NgLbpB complexes with Lf had an overall RMSD of 3.7 Å, however, an improved RMSD of 1.4 Å when aligning just along the interacting domains (C-lobe of Lf and N-lobe of LbpB), indicating a conserved binding interface between Nm and Ng (Figure 4C and D).
evidence: This is inferred from the structural alignment data.

claim: The N-lobe of Lf in the NgLbpB–Lf cryoEM structure is positioned ~12° relatively to the NmLbpB–Lf crystal structure.
source: Additionally, the N-lobe of Lf in the NgLbpB–Lf cryoEM structure is positioned ~12° relatively to the NmLbpB–Lf crystal structure.
evidence: This is observed by comparing the two structures.

claim: In the NmLbpB–Lf complex, the interaction interface is stabilized by extensive hydrogen bonding and salt bridge interactions encompassing a buried surface area of ~1760.8 Å2.
source: In the NmLbpB–Lf complex, the interaction interface is stabilized by extensive hydrogen bonding and salt bridge interactions encompassing a buried surface area of ~1760.8 Å2 (Supplementary file 1d).
evidence: This is calculated from the crystal structure.

claim: All of the mutations tested (K71, Q73, R135, K140, K143, R193, D204, T209, Y210, R223, and D227) had a significant effect on Lf binding.
source: The results showed that all of the mutations had a significant effect on Lf binding with most resulting in more than ~50% reduction in binding except for mutations Q73E, K143E, and R223E.
evidence: This is supported by ELISA and ITC experimental data.

claim: Mutations R135E, D140K, R193E, D204K, D227K, R135E/R223E, and T209N/Y210K resulted in at least a ~75% reduction in Lf binding.
source: Those having at least a ~75% reduction in binding included R135E, D140K, R193E, D204K, D227K, R135E/R223E, and T209N/Y210K.
evidence: This is supported by ELISA experimental data.

claim: Wild-type NmLbpB binds Lf with a Kd value of 0.14 μM, a ΔH of −15.8 kcal/mol, and an n value of ~1.
source: Representative ITC plots show a Kd value of 0.14 μM for Lf binding to wild-type NmLbpB with a ΔH of −15.8 kcal/mol and an n value of ~1.
evidence: This is supported by ITC experimental data.

claim: ΔH values for all the mutants except for K143E were significantly reduced ranging from −5.4 to −11.8 kcal/mol (R135E, D140K, R193E, and D227K) and accompanied by increases in Kd values ranging from 9- to 115-fold over wild type.
source: Agreeing well with the ELISA analysis, ΔH values for the all the mutants except for K143E were significantly reduced ranging from −5.4 to −11.8 kcal/mol (R135E, D140K, R193E, and D227K) and accompanied by increases in Kd values ranging from 9- to 115-fold over wild type.
evidence: This is supported by ITC experimental data.

claim: The presence of Lfcn produced a small, but reproducible, change in the scattering profile at lower q values in the range of 0.04–0.08 for NmLbpB.
source: To gain more insight into the binding of Lfcn with LbpB, we performed SEC-SAXS experiments with and without Lfcn, finding that the presence of Lfcn produced a small, but reproducible, change in the scattering profile at lower q values in the range of 0.04–0.08 (Figure 2C and D).
evidence: This is supported by SEC-SAXS experimental data shown in Figure 2C and D.

claim: A similar change along lower q values in the range of 0.05–0.07 was observed for the NmLbpB–Lf complex when Lfcn was added.
source: A similar change along lower q values in the range of 0.05–0.07 was also observed for the NmLbpB–Lf complex when Lfcn was added (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by SEC-SAXS experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The SEC-SAXS data support the hypothesis that Lfcn binding is distinct from Lf binding.
source: Together, these data support the hypothesis that Lfcn binding is distinct from Lf binding, further supporting that Lfcn binding is along the C-lobe of LbpB.
evidence: This is inferred from the SEC-SAXS experimental data.

claim: Lfcn binding is along the C-lobe of LbpB.
source: Together, these data support the hypothesis that Lfcn binding is distinct from Lf binding, further supporting that Lfcn binding is along the C-lobe of LbpB.
evidence: This is inferred from the SEC-SAXS data and previous literature.

claim: The C-lobe of NmLbpB contains at least one large strongly electronegative region along loops consisting of residues 372–383, 416–418, and 445–526.
source: An electrostatic surface representation of this region shows it to be highly charged with at least one large strongly electronegative region along loops consisting of residues 372–383, 416–418, and 445–526; a more accurate analysis of the electrostatics here is not possible given the lack of order in the loops (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is observed in the electrostatic surface representation shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Lfcn binds to wild-type NmLbpB with a Kd of 3.7 μM, a ΔH of −11.4 kcal/mol, and an n value of ~1.
source: Our results show that Lfcn binds to wild-type NmLbpB with a Kd of 3.7 μM, a ΔH of −11.4 kcal/mol, and an n value of ~1.
evidence: This is supported by ITC experimental data.

claim: The loop deletions Δ372–383, Δ416–418, Δ561–565, Δ594–599, and Δ665–698 showed only minimal differences in ΔH and no significant change in Kd for Lfcn binding.
source: The loop deletions Δ372–383, Δ416–418, Δ561–565, Δ594–599, and Δ665–698, however, showed only minimal differences in ΔH and no significant change in Kd, except for Δ445–526 (ΔH of −9.6 kcal/mol and a ~2.5-fold increase in Kd).
evidence: This is supported by ITC experimental data.

claim: The loop deletion Δ445–526 showed a ΔH of −9.6 kcal/mol and a ~2.5-fold increase in Kd for Lfcn binding.
source: The loop deletions Δ372–383, Δ416–418, Δ561–565, Δ594–599, and Δ665–698, however, showed only minimal differences in ΔH and no significant change in Kd, except for Δ445–526 (ΔH of −9.6 kcal/mol and a ~2.5-fold increase in Kd).
evidence: This is supported by ITC experimental data.

claim: A double loop-deletion mutant Δ445–526_Δ665–698 showed a significantly reduced ΔH with only barely detectable binding to Lfcn.
source: However, a double loop-deletion mutant Δ445–526_Δ665–698 showed a significantly reduced ΔH with only barely detectable binding.
evidence: This is supported by ITC experimental data.

claim: Two loops (residues 445–526 and 665–698) together contribute to Lfcn binding in LbpB.
source: This confirms that these two loops together contribute to Lfcn binding in LbpB, which is likely mediated by the charged residues they contain.
evidence: This is inferred from the ITC experimental data with loop deletion mutants.

claim: Lf binds to NmLbpB alone with a Kd of 0.45 μM and a ΔH of −15.1 kcal/mol.
source: Our results show that Lf binds to NmLbpB alone with a Kd of 0.45 μM and a ΔH of −15.1 kcal/mol (SI Table S8).
evidence: This is supported by ITC experimental data.

claim: Nearly identical binding parameters are observed for Lf binding to the preformed NmLbpB–Lfcn complex, indicating that the presence of Lfcn has no effect on Lf binding.
source: Nearly identical binding parameters are observed for Lf binding to the preformed NmLbpB–Lfcn complex, indicating that the presence of Lfcn has no effect on Lf binding (Figure 6D and SI Table S8).
evidence: This is supported by ITC experimental data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Lfcn binds to the NmLbpB–Lf complex with a Kd of 7.3 μM and a ΔH of −10.6 kcal/mol.
source: Our earlier results showed that Lfcn binds to NmLbpB alone with a Kd of 3.7 μM and a ΔH of −11.4 kcal/mol, while here we found that Lfcn binds to the NmLbpB–Lf complex with a Kd of 7.3 μM and a ΔH of −10.6 kcal/mol (Figure 6E and SI Table S8).
evidence: This is supported by ITC experimental data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Only ~twofold difference in Kd was observed for Lfcn binding to NmLbpB in the presence versus absence of Lf, with no change in ΔH, indicating that binding of Lfcn to NmLbpB is not disrupted in the presence of Lf.
source: Only ~ twofold difference in Kd was observed here, however, no change in ΔH indicating that binding of Lfcn to NmLbpB is not disrupted in the presence of Lf.
evidence: This is inferred from the ITC experimental data.

claim: The current studies strongly support that LbpB binds Lf in a 1:1 complex, which is demonstrated by SEC, SAXS, X-ray crystal structure, and cryoEM structure.
source: However, our studies here strongly support that LbpB binds Lf in a 1:1 complex, which is demonstrated by our SEC, SAXS, X-ray crystal structure, and cryoEM structure.
evidence: This is supported by multiple experimental techniques.

claim: ITC experiments demonstrate 1:1 binding properties between LbpB and Lf with an n value (molar ratio) of ~1.
source: Further, our ITC experiments also demonstrate 1:1 binding properties with an n value (molar ratio) of ~1.
evidence: This is supported by ITC experimental data.

claim: The current structures align well with the previously reported N-lobe only structure of LbpB (PDB ID 4U9C) with an RMSD of 0.34 Å (for 261 Cα atoms).
source: Our structures align well with the previously reported N-lobe only structure of LbpB (PDB ID 4U9C) with an RMSD of 0.34 Å (for 261 Cα atoms) compared to our NmLbpB crystal structure.
evidence: This is supported by structural alignment.

claim: NmLbpB aligns well with NmTbpB (PDB ID 3V8U) with an overall RMSD of 1.8 Å.
source: Additionally, NmLbpB aligns well with NmTbpB (PDB ID 3V8U) with an overall RMSD of 1.8 Å.
evidence: This is supported by structural alignment.

claim: The interacting lobes from LbpB–Lf and TbpB–Tf (PDB ID 3VE1) have an overall RMSD of 1.4 Å.
source: The interacting lobes from LbpB–Lf and TbpB–Tf (PDB ID 3VE1) have an overall RMSD of 1.4 Å, further evidence that the Lbp and Tbp systems likely share a common mechanism in iron acquisition from their respective host iron-binding proteins (Figure 4—figure supplement 3; Gray-Owen and Schryvers, 1996; Noinaj et al., 2013; Schryvers and Lee, 1989).
evidence: This is supported by structural alignment shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: The Lbp and Tbp systems likely share a common mechanism in iron acquisition from their respective host iron-binding proteins.
source: The interacting lobes from LbpB–Lf and TbpB–Tf (PDB ID 3VE1) have an overall RMSD of 1.4 Å, further evidence that the Lbp and Tbp systems likely share a common mechanism in iron acquisition from their respective host iron-binding proteins (Figure 4—figure supplement 3; Gray-Owen and Schryvers, 1996; Noinaj et al., 2013; Schryvers and Lee, 1989).
evidence: This is inferred from structural similarity and supported by citations.

claim: Surface anchored LbpB would selectively accumulate iron-bound Lf, preserving the bound iron for eventual import by LbpA.
source: Here, surface anchored LbpB would selectively accumulate iron-bound Lf, preserving the bound iron for eventual import by LbpA (Figures 3G and 6F; Calmettes et al., 2012).
evidence: This is inferred from the structural data and supported by citation and Figures 3G and 6F.

claim: TbpA (and likely LbpA) can also bind with high affinity apo-Tf/Lf which lacks iron.
source: This would ensure efficiency in iron scavenging for survival during pathogenesis since TbpA (and likely LbpA) can also bind with high affinity apo-Tf/Lf which lacks iron (Krell et al., 2003; Noinaj et al., 2012b; Powell et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Lfcn specifically interacts with the C-lobe only of LbpB through primarily two loops consisting of residues 445–526 and 665–698.
source: Together, our structural studies, mutagenesis, and binding studies agree with the earlier reports and allow us to conclude that Lfcn specifically interacts with the C-lobe only of LbpB through primarily two loops consisting of residues 445–526 and 665–698.
evidence: This is supported by mutagenesis and ITC experimental data.

claim: The presence of Lf had little effect on the binding of Lfcn and vice versa, demonstrating that each have non-overlapping and non-competing binding sites.
source: The presence of Lf had little effect on the binding of Lfcn and vice versa, demonstrating that each have non-overlapping and non-competing binding sites, refuting the previous notion that both may share a common binding site (Brooks et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by ITC experimental data.

claim: The current findings refute the previous notion that Lf and Lfcn may share a common binding site on LbpB.
source: The presence of Lf had little effect on the binding of Lfcn and vice versa, demonstrating that each have non-overlapping and non-competing binding sites, refuting the previous notion that both may share a common binding site (Brooks et al., 2014).
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data and contradicts a previous study.

claim: The current studies support a model where LbpB serves a dual function in Neisserial pathogenesis, in both iron import under iron-limiting conditions and as an antimicrobial peptide sink for the evasion of host immune responses.
source: Together, our studies support a model where LbpB serves a dual function in Neisserial pathogenesis, in both iron import under iron-limiting conditions and as an antimicrobial peptide sink for the evasion of host immune responses (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is supported by the structural and binding data presented in the manuscript and shown in Figure 6F.

claim: NmLbpB alone tends to aggregate in solution as shown by static SAXS analysis.
source: Static small-angle X-ray scattering (SAXS) analysis showed that NmLbpB alone tends to aggregate in solution, while the NmLbpB–Lf complex forms a monodisperse stable complex (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by static SAXS experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The NmLbpB–Lf complex forms a monodisperse stable complex as shown by static SAXS analysis.
source: Static small-angle X-ray scattering (SAXS) analysis showed that NmLbpB alone tends to aggregate in solution, while the NmLbpB–Lf complex forms a monodisperse stable complex (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by static SAXS experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The calculated SAXS scattering curve from the NmLbpB crystal structure agrees well with the experimental SAXS scattering curve in solution.
source: Further, the calculated SAXS scattering curve from our crystal structure agrees well with our experimental SAXS scattering curve in solution (Figure 2H1).
evidence: This is supported by Crysol analysis shown in Figure 2H.

claim: The NmLbpB–Lf interface is stabilized by extensive hydrogen bonding and salt bridge interactions.
source: In the NmLbpB–Lf complex, the interaction interface is stabilized by extensive hydrogen bonding and salt bridge interactions encompassing a buried surface area of ~1760.8 Å2 (Supplementary file 1d).
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure.

claim: The NgLbpB–Lf interface has a buried surface area of 1604 Å2.
source: A zoomed view of the binding interface shows extensive interactions along an elongated surface covering both the C1 and C2 domains of Lf (buried surface area 1604 Å2).
evidence: This is calculated from the cryoEM structure as shown in Figure 4D.
